column2: Between the hours of 1.00 o'clock a.m. and 3.00 o'clock a.m. of June 30, 1967, was an officer or staff member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in the vicinity of an area locally referred to as the Glacier Gulch road which is about 3 or 4 miles from the community of Smithers, B.C., and, if so, what is the name of and rank held by the particular officer or the staff member referred to?
Did the said member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police remove his revolver from his holster and, if so, for what purpose?

2, 3, 4 and 5. Between the hours of 1 and 3 o'clock a.m. on June 30, 1967, Constable Gary Bertwin Schuett of the R.C.M. Police, acting as a provincial peace officer under the contract between the governments of Canada and British Columbia, was investigating suspected contraventions of the provincial liquor laws in the area known as Glacier Gulch road near Smithers, B.C. When members of the group of young people from the Smithers area whom he was investigating began to flee, Constable Schuett drew his service revolver, fired a shot into the air and ordered the suspects to halt. He then gave chase, returning his revolver to its holster as he did so. He had to abandon the chase and return to Smithers for medical attention due to an injury he received in the course of the investigation.

Drury (Minister of Industry):,Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production,QUESTIONS,QUALIFYING STATISTICS FOR MANPOWER CENTRES,,(a) The Timmins and North Bay Canada manpower centres were recognized as components of an economic region consisting of the Canada manpower centres of Kirkland Lake, North Bay, New Liskeard and Timmins. The region registered a negative annual average change in employment of 2.0 per cent. Individually the corresponding percentage change in employment was, as follows: Kirkland Lake -9.1, North Bay -0.6, New Liskeard 2.8 and Timmins -2.8. Accordingly, the areas of Timmins and North Bay qualified for designation either when considered individually or as components of a region under the criterion pertaining to designation of such areas and regions in which for the most recent five years there has been a decline in the level of employment, (b) The Canada manpower centre area of Brandon with an average nonfarm family income of $4,189 qualified under the criterion providing for the designation of such areas in which the average non-farm family income is below $4,250.

The community of Minnedosa lies within Census Division 10 and within a portion that forms part of the Canada manpower centre area of Portage la Prairie. The latter as a Canada manpower centre area does not qualify for designation, however, census division 10 with an average non-farm family income of $3,900 and being contiguous to the designated Canada manpower centre area of Dauphin qualifies under the provision for designating census divisions in which the annual average non-farm family income is below $4,250 and providing they are contiguous to areas that are designated, (c) The Canada manpower centre area of Midland was recognized as a component of an economic region comprised of the areas of Parry Sound, Bracebridge, Midland, Collingwood and Owen
Ociober 11, 1967

Sound. This region had an average non-farm family income of $4,241. Accordingly, the area of Midland qualified for designation under the provision for the grouping of Canada manpower centre areas traditionally recognized as a distinct geographic and economic region and which, considered as a whole, met the criterion relating to the designation of such areas having an average non-farm family income below $4,250.

Comparable statistics for the four Canada manpower centres of Fort Frances, Fort William, Kenora and Port Arthur individually and grouped are as follows: Average annual percentage change in employment growth- Fort Frances 1.6, Fort William 2.5, Kenora 9.6, Port Arthur 1.2, and grouped as an economic region 2.9. Average non-farm family income-Fort Frances $5,114, Fort William $5,440, Kenora $4,966, Port Arthur $5,480, and grouped as an economic region $5,321.

Is the government planning the issue of economic guide lines to those whose activities have the greatest influence on the cost of living, as one means of trying to stem the rapid increase in the cost of living?

,Progressive Conservative,,George Harris Hees,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e268685f-5f98-4956-a0d4-9aaefd036337&Language=E&Section=ALL

Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Finance):,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,QUESTIONS,THE CANADIAN ECONOMY,STEPS TO MEET INCREASE IN COST OF LIVING,As I said in the house the other day, the government is giving consideration to an organized campaign to mobilize public opinion in favour of greater stability in costs and prices, and I have invited all those concerned to be considering this question. I hope they are doing so and will be discussing with us and among themselves how best this might be carried out. Whether this would be called guide lines I am not certain, but when the government itself has taken the necessary fiscal action I would hope to have the cooperation of the public, organized management and labour in stabilizing more effectively than hitherto increases in prices and costs.

,Liberal,,Mitchell William Sharp,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0ae975c1-8187-4ab9-b0ff-dfe9da639543&Language=E&Section=ALL

view of the fact that the cost of living has risen more rapidly in Canada than in almost any other western country, according to an O.E.C.D. report, does the minister's program include the setting up of a prices review board to gather information as to the relationship between corporation profits, consumer prices and incomes in Canada?

,New Democratic Party,,Thomas Clement (Tommy) Douglas,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d34eb71d-3bc8-4258-8a3f-2007fa662c38&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,Mitchell William Sharp,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0ae975c1-8187-4ab9-b0ff-dfe9da639543&Language=E&Section=ALL

George Hees (Northumberland):,,THE BUDGET,ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,"Mr. Speaker, today this country faces a very serious economic situation from three points of view. The first is the rapid deterioration of the purchasing power of our dollar, which has reached such a point that next January 1, $1.05 will be required to buy the same amount of goods and services which $1 could buy last January 1. This is hard on all citizens of this country, but particularly so on those who live on fixed incomes, such as pensioners, because they have no way of increasing their income to meet this rise in the cost of living by new wage contracts or by increasing the price of their goods to other Canadians.

Second, we have a critical housing shortage. This year the housing production will fall short by more than 50,000 units of the minimum of 190,000 housing units which the Economic Council of Canada has advised us is the absolute minimum we must produce in a year to provide adequately for the housing needs of our citizens.

Third, a rapidly deereasing industrial productivity is facing us as we prepare to enter the most serious economic competition we have ever faced, which will be presented to us starting on January 1 when the Kennedy round tariff reductions come into effect. All Canadian producers will face much stiffer competition as a result of the fact that foreign goods will enter our markets more cheaply. Although tariffs against Canadian goods in the export markets will be reduced, those tariffs will also be reduced against the products of our competitors, and the home producers will not sit back and simply allow us to take over, any more than Canadian producers will allow foreign producers to take over this market. Therefore, at a time when we are facing the most serious competition we have ever faced, we are in a very weak position.

Not only must we correct these three situations that I have mentioned, but we must make sure that they do not recur in the future. To do so we must first of all find out why these situations have occurred, and take steps to make sure the same does not happen in the future.
The first cause of this trouble was the lack of skilled workers, which became apparent in
October 11, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Hees

the latter part of 1964. In 1961 the Conservative government introduced a policy of building training schools across this country. During the next two years, we built no less than 224 new schools, and enlarged 130 existing schools. This gave the country an added capacity for turning out trained skilled workers to the extent of 140,000 trained people a year. We had planned a systematic increase in this building program, year by year, to look after the growing demand for skilled workers in the future. However, when the Liberal government came to office in 1963, they were not aware of the growing importance of providing greater numbers of skilled workers for our factories and our farms, and they did not continue this expansion program at the rate we had planned. The result was that in the latter half of 1964, it became obvious that a very real shortage of skilled workers was developing in this country. As I have said, the government did nothing to increase the rate of expansion which we had planned when we were in office, nor did it increase immigration to bring in the additional skilled workers whom our industry required to fill the gap between the numbers we were turning out from our training schools, and the number we needed in this country. As a result of this shortage of skilled workers, our factories and farms were unable to produce goods in quantities necessary to meet the demands of the affluent society here in Canada and in countries abroad. Prices started to rise, and inflation set in.

We know that inflation is caused when too much money is chasing too few goods. There are two ways to correct the situation. The first is to increase the volume of goods available for sale. The second is to decrease the amount of money available to buy the goods. As you would expect, this government chose the latter course, namely the negative course, and applied a tight money policy with regard to our country's economy, as a result of which interest rates began to rise.

Because of the government's tight money policy, our producers were unable to carry out the expansion of plants and equipment to handle the need for increased production. In addition, the shortage of skilled workers continued. Goods remained in short supply. As a result of these two situations, prices continued to rise, and have continued to do so ever since, until today we have the highest cost of living in our history.
Because of this government's tight money policy, mortgage money has become very scarce since the fall of 1965. As a result, in

1966 the number of housing starts in this country fell 20 per cent lower than in the previous year. This year, because of the same conditions as experienced in 1966, the number of housing starts will remain the same as last year, and we will be more than 50,000 houses short of the minimum of 190,000 starts which the Economic Council of Canada tells us is the absolute minimum we must produce in this country each year to look after our country's minimum housing needs.

As a result of the shortage of capital, of the shortage of skilled workers in this country to meet the demand for products, and of the high interest rates which have impeded the ability of producers to modernize their plants and equipment and introduce new systems into their production, our productivity has fallen very seriously at a time when we face the most serious competition we have ever faced, brought about, as I have said, by the Kennedy round tariff reductions which will come into effect next January.

So we are faced with a very serious situation indeed, and it is the responsibility of members of this parliament to advise the government as to what we believe should be done to overcome and improve this situation, because it is obvious from the government's lack of action, and lack of policy in this regard, that they are unable to meet this very serious situation.

Over the past 25 years, Mr. Speaker, we in this parliament have devoted the major portion of our thought and energy to developing a social security system; one which today gives reasonable coverage to those who cannot provide for themselves. In the future these measures will certainly be expanded and improved as we are able to pay for such expansion out of our national income. But in the meantime I believe we should devote our major thought and energy to developing an economic climate in this country in which industry and agriculture can expand according to their ability to sell their products at prices which people, both in Canada and in the export markets are willing to pay. It is only in this way that we can make available the jobs which our people need to keep them employed; and that we can pay for the social security that we have given ourselves; and provide the best form of social security of all, namely, good jobs for all of our people, with an expanding future.
Such an economic climate must include five things: first, a greatly increased productivity;
October 11. 1967

second, a continuous flow of credit and mortgage money at reasonable rates of interest; third, a stable and, if possible, declining tax rate; fourth, an adequate supply of skilled workers so that our factories and our farms may produce up to the demand of consumers for their products; and fifth, a far greater research effort to develop new and better products at lower costs.

How are we going to produce such a climate, Mr. Speaker? I believe the first step is to discard the present lack of economic planning indulged in by this government, which causes it to move from crisis to crisis, and to substitute for that lack of economic planning the direction and planning that is needed to guide our economy along the most productive lines.

This can be brought about by replacing the unco-ordinated effort of the six departments of government which have the greatest effect on our economy, namely the Department of Finance, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the Department of Industry, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Transport and the Department of Manpower and Immigration, with a co-ordinated planning effort.

The instrument for carrying out this future planning would be a permanent committee of the cabinet, to be known as the economic planning committee, under the chairmanship of the Minister of Finance, and composed, along with the minister, of the ministers of the other five departments to which I have referred. This committee would work closely with the Canadian Economic Council, and would rely heavily on its economic studies in preparing the recommendations which it would put forward to the cabinet and the Prime Minister in relation to the future economic growth of this country.

These plans; the results to be expected from them; and their cost, will give the government vitally needed information on which to base the decisions that they will have to make in the future regarding spending priorities when the annual budget is prepared each year and whenever any other important economic consultations take place.

One of the first tasks with which this committee would have to busy itself would be the development of increased productivity in manufacturing, which is a major employer. Measured in terms of output per person employed in manufacturing, our performance over the 20 years between 1946 and 1966 inclusive showed an average yearly increase
The Budget-Mr. Hees

of 3.4 per cent. This year the preliminary figures available to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics clearly indicate that the rate of increase in the work force has exceeded the rate of increase in manufacturing production, and that our present productivity is considerably below that of last year.

In 1961 the Conservative government established the productivity council, which was made up of representatives of industry and labour. All those representatives were extremely able men chosen for their ability in their particular field; and I might add that one of the distinguished members of this council was the present Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), who did very able work for the council. The job of the council was to recommend steps which they considered would most likely increase productivity.

During the next two years, this Productivity Council made excellent progress, but unfortunately in 1963, when the Liberal party took over the government, the Productivity Council was disbanded, and the Department of Industry was created to take the place of the industrial section of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the Department of Defence Production.

This new department took over responsibility for increasing productivity from the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I think it would be interesting, Mr. Speaker, for us now to examine the results this new department has been able to produce since it took over this very important responsibility from the productivity council, operating under the aegis of the Department of Trade and Commerce.

These results, Mr. Speaker, are as follows. Productivity increased in 1964 over 1963 by 4.3 per cent. It increased in the following year, 1965, over 1964 by 4 per cent. It increased last year, 1966, over 1965 by only 2 per cent, while productivity in the United States increased over the year before by 3.6 per cent. And as I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, the preliminary figures available to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics indicate very clearly that productivity this year is falling very considerably below that of a year ago.

So, Mr. Speaker, we see that the performance of the department which took responsibility for increasing productivity away from the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the productivity council, has been to reduce the rate of productivity growth in four years from 4.3 per cent a year
the moving from crisis to crisis which we have experienced lately.

I have tried to outline to the house in the brief time allotted to me why we have arrived at the position we occupy today. We have runaway inflation, a housing crisis and a shocking drop in productivity. That is not good enough for a country with Canada's potential. There is an additional reason for our troubles, and I sympathize with the Minister of Finance sincerely in this regard. The minister is not given a proper opportunity to do the job that I think he would like to do. It became obvious, to anyone who did not know it before and who listened to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) speaking in the house the other night, that we have not one minister of finance in this government, but two. We have the minister of finance for Eglinton and the minister of finance for Davenport. It was obvious, as the minister of finance for Davenport spoke the other night, that he completely disagreed with the minister of finance for Eglinton. That kind of approach to this country's problems is not good enough. The trouble is that the two ministers cannot get their points of view across to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). Thank heaven the President of the Privy Council is not minister of finance; obviously he is trying to be and this, I believe, is causing a great deal of confusion in this government.

I urge the Minister of Finance to take a strong stand and to outline to the house before this debate ends what he intends to do, regardless of what the President of the Privy Council has to say. He should tell us whether he intends to make available to industry in this country a taxation incentive to enable it to buy new labour saving machinery and labour saving systems which are needed to bring costs down. Such machinery and systems are needed if productivity in this country is not to drop, as it has been doing, day by day.

I urge him to take a strong stand with other members of the cabinet to do the things I believe he would like to do. If this government does not intend to take action it will become ever more clear that the country cannot afford to put up with an administration which is overtaken by events day by day; we need a government which shapes events. The only cheering factor in this whole dim picture today is that, fortunately, time will make it possible for this country in the relatively
The Budget-Mr. Otto
near future to have such a government to carry on its affairs.

,Progressive Conservative,,George Harris Hees,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=e268685f-5f98-4956-a0d4-9aaefd036337&Language=E&Section=ALL
2505944,ca.proc.d.1967-10-11.21.1.3,1967-10-11,4deee6dc-295b-44ee-83b9-04cbe06ba653,ca.m.9441,Mr. Steven Otto (York East):,,THE BUDGET,ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,This discussion prompts me to debate a few points with the minister. It is sometimes presumed that I take issue with ministers and criticize them. Of course, this is not the case. In this instance I do not intend to criticize the minister because I sympathize with his point of view.

If I may introduce a personal note, I was much impressed by the manner in which the hon. gentleman introduced his subject; he reminded me very much of his father-in-law who was my high school teacher in St. James, Manitoba. I may say the minister made a presentation which would do his father-inlaw great credit. Rather than take issue with the hon. gentleman I will comment on some of the points he made. I think he is on the right track if he is a reform minister-and this is a reform party and a reform government. The first requisite is to understand our assumptions correctly; we all base our ideas on certain assumptions. The minister made a meaningful statement when he said it was surprising to find at a time of easy money like the present that high interest rates were prevalent, because the book says that in times of easy money we should have low interest rates.

It is very important to understand that something has happened to an assumption, because we are then free to base our actions on that new understanding. Today we have high interest rates even in a time of easy money, and I dare say that even if interest rates on mortgages were raised the desired result would not be produced. The minister told us, more or less, that inflation or expected inflation causes investors to become concerned about the real values of long term bonds and leads them to demand higher yields as compensation. This is of course true. But I doubt whether high yields would solve the problem. My hon. friend also pointed out that the result is a desire for liquidity. That also is true; people do not want to invest their money for 25 years if they are convinced in their own minds that the inflationary process will offset their returns. I was greatly surprised when in accordance with this concept the N.H.A. mortgage interest rate was raised to 8-J per cent in an attempt to outguess investors who do not wish to put money into long term investments.
I intend to mention a few more assumptions and I should like the minister to examine them with me. It has now been proved
October 11, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Otto

wrong to assume that easy money is accompanied by low interest rates. This leads me to wonder how many other assumptions may prove equally misleading. The minister's answer is as follows: If, collectively and individually, labour and management do not exercise restraint in connection with wage and price increases, there will be no escape from a cooling off period. There is a presumption here that if we do not exercise restraint higher taxes will be imposed in order to resolve the problem of inflation.

This is based on the assumption that higher taxes would mean lower take-home pay and less desire to spend money, because there would be less money to spend. But I would ask the minister this: Does the working man take account of his total annual income, or does he simply look at his take-home pay? I suggest he is not really concerned what his income is, or what his wage is; he does not really care how much is taken away in taxation. What he wants is a take-home pay sufficient to buy the goods for which he and others like him have created a demand.

,Liberal,,Steven Otto,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4deee6dc-295b-44ee-83b9-04cbe06ba653&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,Mitchell William Sharp,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=0ae975c1-8187-4ab9-b0ff-dfe9da639543&Language=E&Section=ALL
2505946,ca.proc.d.1967-10-11.21.1.5,1967-10-11,4deee6dc-295b-44ee-83b9-04cbe06ba653,ca.m.9441,Mr. Olto:,,THE BUDGET,ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,I shall deal later with the question of the voluntary exercise of restraint. I say that take-home pay is the real issue, not the total hourly or weekly wage. If the workingman does not get enough to spend, he will ask for more.

This leads to another question. Will he get more? Normally, at the time the books were written, demand and desire were two different things. A man might desire a new television set or a new car but if he did not have the money to pay for it he could not buy it. Demand was governed completely and directly by purchasing power. I do not think the minister will deny that today desire and demand have come very close together, because the producers of goods have so merged the two that desire for an object creates a demand for it. That is the whole purpose of promotional advertising. If the demand is strong enough, other methods are used in order to get the purchasing power. This of course is where we run into trouble.

The minister has just asked whether voluntary restriction is something we can anticipate. I shall be a little more pragmatic. Organized labour-and we are talking mainly about organized labour-is not dealing on the basis of long term considerations. It does not
have the same vested interest in a particular industry, or a particular plant, as it once did. There is greater movement.

I will give an example. Some five or six years ago Mr. Reuther of the automotive workers union pondered the problem of leisure time. He decided to adopt a policy of cultural education, cultural improvement for his union members, anticipating the time when they would have more leisure. It was quite a program. There were television commentaries about it and it was written up in the press. He was going to spend $20 million of the union money to build cultural centres where members could improve their minds and be ready for the anticipated greater leisure time.

However, this was a very short dream. It was shot down very quickly, and Mr. Reuther has not mentioned the subject since, simply because labour is interested in short term gains. Union members want more money; they want more purchasing power. If one examines labour negotiations over the past three or four years he finds that the emphasis has shifted back to money. Labour says, ""We don't care about the side benefits, we want more money.""

The minister's plea to organized labour for restraint and for adoption of the long term point of view will receive a doubtful reception, to say the least. But this does not exonerate management. Management classes of all types are looking more and more to the side benefits. They are not concerned about salary. They are concerned about memberships in social clubs, golf clubs, diners clubs, travel, entertainment and such things as that. Salary is not the great issue.

Another assumption upon which we base our thinking is that there is compulsion on all sides to settle work stoppages. Work stoppages have a great deal to do with production, something the hon. gentleman from Northumberland (Mr. Hees) has been talking about. We presume that when there is a work stoppage both sides want to settle it. We presume unions do not like giving out strike pay and that companies desire to start making money again. But this is only a presumption. We know today that unions have adjusted very nicely to such a situation, and one thinks immediately of the current example of the Ford work stoppage.
Workers at Ford are on strike and the automotive workers union is willing to pay $20 million to support the strike. Today if a
October 11, 1967

firm is struck, and this happened recently during the iron workers strike in Toronto, the workers can go and work elsewhere, be it in a union shop or not. They get a certificate enabling them to do this, but in order to get that certificate they have to pay back to their union 50 cents for each hour they work. Thus there is no longer the same compulsion on a union to settle a strike.

Let us consider management in such a situation. Recently the Registrar General (Mr. Turner) wrote an article pointing out that the shareholding structure of large corporations is very fluid. Within a period of six months those with shares will often sell them. Shares are used as a means of speculation. We have developed a new managerial class which is not too greatly concerned with the profit position.

Recently I spoke to a group of managers, one of whom argued that a work stoppage now is really a game of inventory. Management tries to produce enough inventory to make a strike ineffective, and of course the union tries to do the opposite. On top of this the same gentleman said, ""It really does not matter much, because if we did produce 12 months of the year we would have to get a new sales manager since the present one cannot sell 12 months production. It is simpler for him to have only nine or ten months production.""

Indirectly management is not that keen about increasing production because this increases its distribution problem. What we have is an assumption that is wrong. Our assumption is that management tries to produce and negotiate a settlement immediately. We also assume that labour tries to negotiate a settlement immediately. This has proven not to be so. Directly or indirectly this situation has developed and we must examine what we can do to overcome it.

There is what I would term the psychology of business and finance with respect to a shortage of money. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) has quite rightly said that business and finance must consider which choice to adopt. I would go further and ask the minister to delve deeper into the matter and see whether a certain psychology established by industry or by finance cannot be overcome by government departmental activity.

If I as an investor believe inflation is going to increase by 5 per cent per year, naturally I want to invest my money over a short period. If I invest it for 25 years I will want 75 per cent interest to cover the rise in inflation. To combat this the government at present will
The Budget-Mr. Otto
try to get me to loosen my money and allow me to charge a higher interest rate. But here I will run into competition with the government. It is like a Dutch auction.

I suggest that, where business is confident, it will expand its activity even if it has to borrow money at 20 per cent. The minister and his department may try to cool this trend; but which is going to be stronger, government or business? This is something worth investigating.

National guide lines have been talked about for business, industry and labour. Guide lines are all very well, but I have always been impressed by a quotation which says that only the earned profits are credited-the unearned profits have gone down to defeat.

The government may tell an industry to behave properly. But if the people running it do behave properly and in the interests of Canada, then I suggest that is not the business in which they should be, because essentially all business is out to make money. Capital today is an international thing. It flows quickly from border to border, from nation to nation. If the climate is not suitable in one place it will move to another place. It will try to do as good a job as possible in the country where it is invested, but its primary concern is to make profits. There is always a certain friction. The choice is; Shall we be good citizens of Canada, or shall we put our money into Tanganyika or some other place where we can make more profit?

Another assumption to which the minister and the hon. member for Northumberland have often referred is that savings are the key to industrial and commercial expansion. I put it to the minister, whether people really use savings, in the term that we know, to invest in equity stock, or whether they use their savings to buy insurance, bonds and real estate mortgages. I would ask him to investigate whether it is not really dividends, profits, that go back into industrial expansion. If this be the case then it does not matter that Canada is short of savings so long as we can somehow recapture dividends that might leave the country and have them reinvested in Canada. I believe it is dividends which are more likely than savings to be reinvested in capital expansion.

I should like to make a number of suggestions to the minister. I make them not only to the Minister of Finance, but of course to every minister of this government, because these things are very interrelated. The first in
October 11, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Otto

order of priority is that we must recognize that we cannot increase wages or social benefits, or any such things, more than the increase in the gross national product. If we increase our gross national product by 10 per cent, then we can spend only 10 per cent, whether it is in increased wages, whether it is in welfare payments or in some other form. If we spend more than the increase in the gross national product, then the government goes broke whether it happens immediately or later.

A nation cannot spend more than it earns. If our production increases 10 per cent we can only consume 10 per cent more goods. The government therefore must devise immediately a way to settle wage disputes and management-labour contracts without work stoppages. This is not so new. We have had the same type of wage dispute settlement procedures for 100 years.

Surely we can induce management to settle a strike, even if it means going to management and saying that for so long as the strike continues every dollar the company makes will be attached, so that at least the company does not lose anything and does not make anything, but production continues and the government is the beneficiary. We may have to go to labour and say to them that so long as a strike lasts their union dues will go to the government. Surely we have reached a time when we can solve this problem by introducing a procedure for negotiation of labour disputes, without the necessity of a work stoppage, because it is the production stoppage which causes the trouble. It really does not matter if our new technology enables us to increase our production by 10 per cent, if we lose 10 per cent as a result of the work stoppage. One nullifies the other. There are many ways this can be handled, but surely some way must be found.

Then there is the matter of consumer credit. This somehow or other must be brought under control. The minister might say that we will cut down wages by taxation, so that automatically people will not be able to buy the goods they wish to buy. But we have a fantastically large industry which actually is in the business of usury. This is very old. They will say, ""Oh, no; buy now, pay later"". They will say that they will anticipate the earning capacity. So it really does not matter what the minister or the government says, so long as the consumer credit industry has faith in the economy or has faith in collecting a certain amount of money. Since they charge 18 per cent they have a leeway there for bad
[Mr. Ottc.l

debts. They will make the purchasing power available. Somehow this other source of banking must be brought under the same control the banks are under at the present time, whether it is under the Bank of Canada or under some other department of government. Any industry or agency which creates or plays with money must be brought under government control, if the government is to exercise control over the economy.

As to the matter of taxation, I may say that I have studied the Carter report, and I think the minister will come to the conclusion that most of the recommendations of the Carter commission will have to be adopted. I hate to say this, because it is contrary to my thinking about the establishment, but Mr. Carter could be described as the top member of the establishment. I sometimes think it is a shame that only the top member of the reactionary establishment should be the one to introduce a scheme which is necessary and radical. I think that, with the introduction of the Carter report, we could look forward to increased production and buoyancy of financial institutions. I think we would have taxation powers which would enable us to shift emphasis from industry to industry in accordance with government policy. We must make new arrangements in respect of exports and imports. I have introduced a bill on that subject which would enable us to balance exports and imports by production hours rather than by money.

Another idea which at least should be investigated is the matter of escalation of bonds, and possibly the escalation of mortgages. So long as investors are not willing to invest money for a long term period because they are afraid of inflation, then of course indirectly they want to introduce inflation to justify their own ideas. We might say to the Canadian investor that if today he invests in a government bond in the amount of $100, in ten years time we will pay him the $100 plus the cost of living index. At least this would give the government some measure of control over the desirability of taking in or putting out money. At the moment, however, so long as the investor, whether small or large, thinks we are on the road to inflation he will not invest and will not put up long term securities.

This is not new. An eastern company now is working with a United States company in the institution of an idea of insurance policies which will escalate. We have yet to see what the reaction will be, but I imagine it will be very successful. There is no reason why the
October 11, 1967
government could not take a lead in investigating what would be the result of such a policy.

There should be a reorganization of our whole government structure in respect of insurance and welfare. Is our unemployment insurance really an insurance policy, or is it a welfare policy; is it payable merely to those who lose their jobs or is it payable because of certain other circumstances? Is it under the influence of politics? Of course it is. Do people look on unemployment insurance as savings? In other words, when they have had the good fortune never to have been laid off and are now ready to retire, do they say to themselves, ""That is my money, I want it"" So long as they do that we do not have an insurance policy; we have a welfare policy.

Many other items of government could be reorganized and placed in their proper brackets. We should know what is insurance and what is welfare, so that we know where we stand. Insurance should stand on its own feet, whether it is national housing insurance, unemployment insurance or hospital insurance, including the old age pension. It should stand on its own feet, so that we know what amount we can afford to give to other welfare measures.

There is also the matter of the Canada Development Corporation, but I believe I have dealt with the necessity for this. I have also introduced a measure in this regard. Of course all of this is as easy or as difficult as the minister or we as a government have the guts to make it. I was looking at a book written back in the early fifteenth century by a gentleman named Machiavelli, who was much maligned in past centuries. He was giving instructions to Lorenzo the Magnificent in respect of how to run his policies. I was interested to find that at that time, when instructing Lorenzo the Magnificent about the difficulty of introducing new ideas, he said:

And it ought to be remembered that there is nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct, or more uncertain in its success, than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things.

Because the innovator has for enemies all those who have done well under the old conditions, and lukewarm defenders in those who may do well under the new. This coolness arises partly from fear of the opponents, who have the laws on their side, and partly from the incredulity of men, who do not readily believe in new things until they have had a long experience of them.
The same principle applies to those measures introduced to the house by way of reforms in the rules and procedures of this

The Budget-Mr. Gregoire place. Let me remind the minister that in order to introduce reform you must introduce new ideas. This will be difficult, in that the department will oppose because it is so sure of the value of old methods. This is particularly so when you can find in any book on economics the statement in black and white that when you have a lot of money you will have low interest rates.

The hon. gentleman representing Northumberland quoted from the same book and said that when you have too much money chasing too few goods you have inflation. Let me suggest to that hon. gentleman that if he looks back over the past seven years he will find that we had inflation during times of tight money and during times of loose money, yet at all times we had lots of goods.

In order to introduce a new idea you must look back to find out why it is necessary. I put it to the minister that he should look at all the assumptions upon which his department's policies are based. If he finds that those assumptions can remain unchanged, that is good; but if he finds that the assumptions are wrong by today's standards, then he requires new ideas and new rules, not those in the book.

,Liberal,,Steven Otto,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4deee6dc-295b-44ee-83b9-04cbe06ba653&Language=E&Section=ALL
2505947,ca.proc.d.1967-10-11.21.1.6,1967-10-11,acd5380d-f564-427d-821a-4528ecdba8f3,ca.m.9577,Mr. Gilles Gregoire (Lapointe):,,THE BUDGET,ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few remarks today concerning some statements that have been made, some events that have taken place and the atmosphere that exists at this time in Quebec.
First, I would like to comment on a sentence spoken yesterday by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). As recorded in Hansard in the right-hand column of page 2,967 he said:

I do know one think. Our confederation was founded in 1867. Since that time I am convinced that Canadians of all extractions recognize the right of bilingualism in our country, namely the French and English languages. That is the wish of the people.

Now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Villeneuve admits that the people want bilingualism and recognize the rights of bilingualism. But what surprises me is that the member for Villeneuve adds that since confederation, Canadians of all origins recognize the right of bilingualism in our country.

Now, what are the facts? Exactly what has happened? Confederation was voted in 1867. Barely four years later, as early as in 1871, in New Brunswick, an act abolishes Catholic schools and banishes French as an official language in New Brunswick.
October 11, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Gregoire

Six years later, in 1877, an act in Prince Edward Island forbids the use of French in the schools throughout the province. A fine start for the first hundred years of confederation; barely ten years later, in 1877, the use of French in the schools is forbidden by a provincial law.

Thirteen years later, in 1890, in spite of section 23 of the Manitoba Act, out west, that province abolishes separate schools and the official use of the French language. A further interdiction in another province, Manitoba, in 1890.

In 1905, Laurier sacrifices the rights of French minorities in Saskatchewan and Alberta, under section 17 of the Saskatchewan Act and under section 17 of the Alberta Act (1905). Everything was going well for the rights of the French language within confederation.
In 1912, confessional schools are abolished in Keewatin and French is forbidden. Bilingualism was in a fine shape during the first century of confederation.
In 1912 also, under regulation 17, Ontario goes to war against the French language. As things were, there was some talk of a war against the French language in Ontario.
In 1916, Manitoba abolishes French in all primary schools. Things were going well, a hundred years of confederation. That is why we are probably right in referring to a hundred years of injustice.
In 1930, Anderson, the Saskatchewan premier, banishes French from his province.
So there, all the provinces have done it. French was prohibited by legislation, French was banned, it was prohibited in primary schools in the western provinces, in Ontario and in the maritimes.

The hon. member for Villeneuve said yesterday: it is not because of confederation, it is not Ottawa's fault. Well, Mr. Speaker, there is in the British North America Act, in the Canadian constitution, legislation giving Ottawa the authority which has always been granted to the federal government, to intervene in the cases I have mentioned, when the use of French is banned from a province. Section 93, subsection 3 of the British North America Act which laid down the Canadian confederation, the famous confederation, states:
Where in any Province a System of Separate or Dissentient Schools exists by Law at the Union or is thereafter established by the Legislature of the

Province, an Appeal shall lie to the Governor General in Council from any Act or Decision of any Provincial Authority affecting any Right or Privilege of the Protestant or Roman Catholic Minority of the Queen's Subjects in relation to Education:
It was very simple. And subsection 4 of same section 93 states:

In case any such Provincial Law as from Time to Time seems to the Governor General in Council requisite for the due Execution of the Provisions of this Section is not made, or in case any Decision of the Governor General in Council on any Appeal under this Section is not duly executed by the proper Provincial Authority in that Behalf, then and in every such Case, and as far only as the Circumstances of each Case require, the Parliament of Canada may make remedial Laws for the due Execution of the Provisions of this Section and of any Decision of the Governor General in Council under this Section.

Mr. Speaker, legislation to ban and prohibit the use of French was passed by all provinces and never, never has the Ottawa government invoked the provisions of subsections 3 or 4 of section 93 to adopt remedial measures towards the oppressed minorities in western Canada, in Ontario and in the maritimes. Nor has the federal government felt it proper even to attempt to repair the wrongs to the French minorities in other provinces although it was fully empowered to do so under subsections 3 or 4 of the British North America Act.

Well, is it not the fault of confederation, of the federal government at Ottawa if our minorities have been persecuted as they have been in other provinces? I say yes, Mr. Speaker. I say it is the fault of Ottawa, of the federal government which failed to adopt the remedial measures indicated in section 93.

2505951,ca.proc.d.1967-10-11.21.1.10,1967-10-11,acd5380d-f564-427d-821a-4528ecdba8f3,ca.m.9577,Mr. Gregoire:,,THE BUDGET,ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,Mr. Speaker, at first sight, that may seem to apply to religion rather than to language, but judging from the indirect methods used to prohibit and suppress
October 11, 1967

the use of the French language, it was done under cover of religion and the result is exactly the same. In fact, the provinces that wanted to prohibit the French language in the west succeeded exactly as if the act had mentioned it. They acted indirectly but they achieved exactly the same purpose.
Furthermore, subsection 3 deals with separate or dissident schools. It is not necessarily a matter of religion; it a matter of language as well as religion. Indeed, the following expression is used:
-a system of separate or dissident schools.

What have been the results, Mr. Speaker, of all these discriminatory measures passed in all the provinces, except Quebec, where no such legislation was passed and whose minorities were respected? What have been the consequences? Well, Mr. Speaker, between 1900 and 1961, date of the last census in Canada, 514,312 Canadians of French origin gave up speaking French. That has been a true racial and linguistic genocide.

Those French-speaking Canadians have adopted English as their mother language and 34 per cent of the French Canadians from the other provinces have become Englishspeaking citizens and have forsaken their own language due, precisely, to these discriminatory laws which were passed in the nine other provinces of Canada but not in the province of Quebec.

Let us take Newfoundland, for instance, where in 1961 there were only 3,150 citizens whose mother tongue was French; on the other hand, 14,021 citizens whose mother tongue was French have stopped speaking their own language and have adopted English as their mother tongue; this means, in Newfoundland, a loss of 81.65 per cent.
In British Columbia, 26,179 have declared French as their mother language and 40,791 have given up French in order to adopt English as their mother tongue which means a 60.9 per cent loss.
In Nova Scotia, 48,315 citizens have given up the French language, opting for English as their mother tongue, a loss of 54.9 per cent.
In Prince Edward Island, 9,460 have chosen English rather than French as their mother tongue, so there are only 7,958 people left in Prince Edward Island whose mother tongue is French.
In Alberta, the loss is 41,043 persons, in Saskatchewan, 23,661. In Ontario, 222,639 French-speaking Canadians have abandoned their mother tongue and speak only English,
The Budget-Mr. Gregoire and this just because these laws have been passed. In Manitoba, 23,037 have relinquished their mother tongue, and in New Brunswick, 21,597.

This has been the inevitable result of the various laws I mentioned earlier, which have been passed since confederation against the use of the French language and for its prohibition in other provinces.
For this reason, I think the hon. member for Villeneuve should re-examine the facts before stating, as he did, that:
Since that time, I am convinced that Canadians of all extractions recognize the right of bilingualism in our country, namely the French and English
languages.
This was accepted only in one place, the province of Quebec, and refused by the other nine provinces through laws and discriminatory legislation which led to an actual linguistic and racial genocide.

Mr. Speaker, I reread today the speech made by the hon. member for Villeneuve, and I think his argument contained two specific points. First, he did not think that the present situation in Quebec or in Canada was the fault of confederation or Ottawa.
In my opinion, Ottawa is certainly to blame for the language situation, because it did not take the remedial and other measures necessary.

Even today, Mr. Speaker, in 1967, the Minister of Transport, here in Ottawa, tells us that nothing will be done to facilitate winter navigation on the St. Lawrence, because Halifax might be harmed. Even yesterday, in Toronto, the mayor of that city declared that he did not want Expo to become permanent in Montreal because it would be detrimental to Toronto. This or that action is always being forbidden in Quebec as it might be prejudicial to Halifax, or Toronto, or some other city. Why can the Quebeckers not be allowed to develop on their own, when they have the natural resources, the possibilities to do so?
The St. Lawrence is in Quebec; yet the Quebeckers cannot have winter navigation lest it harm Halifax.
Expo 67 was planned, built and is now a living fact, in Montreal. And all this should be pulled down so that it will not interfere with Toronto.

Is this that national unity you are talking about? To destroy and demolish and prevent Quebec from developing so that other sections of the country may not be harmed. Well, I say that when such things happen in
October 11, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Gregoire Quebec, it is Ottawa's fault, and the blame should also be put on confederation; they prefer to please Toronto and Halifax rather than to allow Quebec to develop.

This situation has been prevailing in Canada for the past hundred years and that is why I say that we are quite justified in Quebec, in view of laws and facts I have just mentioned to cry out: a hundred years of injustice!

Mr. Speaker, another matter raised now by the hon. member for Villeneuve and raised by him in Quebec over the weekend-and I think he is right and I agree with him-is that there is no political freedom without economic freedom. But he should finish his sentence by adding that there is no economic freedom without political freedom, and if Quebec wants economic freedom, it shall need its political freedom also, just as it will have to work towards economic freedom to attain political freedom.

Mr. Speaker, I have here a few figures. We hear sometimes of the hopes of the people of Quebec, and of their desire to develop in some spheres. Well, I have here some statistics which show that confederation as a whole has not always served the aspirations, desires or wishes of Quebec, far from it.
Take, for instance, Canada's national debt, which I divide into four separate stages. I shall mention them first, then give an explanation of each afterwards.
First, in 1840, at the time of the Union Act; second, the British war in South Africa; third, the First World War; and fourth, the Second World War.
Our national debt arose out of those four stages, but there was also the Korean war.

The year 1840 saw the passage of the Union Act, under which Upper Canada and Lower Canada were united, although the latter, now Quebec, had about 40 per cent more population than the former, now Ontario. Ottawa decided then to take over the debts of both provinces, of both groups. The debt was about twelve times higher in Ontario with a sparser population than in Quebec, but everything was put in the same package and they said: The others got into debt-you, to a lesser degree-but you will pay part of Ontario's debts in agreeing to the Union Act.

When confederation became effective, the debts of Ontario, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia were all lumped together, and Quebec was forced to assume part of it; thus Ottawa started in 1867 with a $93,046,502 debt, and

Quebec was forced to assume its share, even though this came from the other three provinces. Then the debt remained at a rather steady level until 1913, that is for a period of 46 years. In 1913, it rose from $93 million to $483 million. In 1914, war was declared and when it was over in 1920, the debt had increased eightfold and stood at $3,041 million. Then for 19 years the debt remained stable, barely increasing; it went up from $3,041 to $3,710 million. And yet Canada was going through a period of economic crisis, of unemployment, of dole, of misery. In spite of all that, the debt did not go up. It increased eightfold in six years during the first world war but during the 19 years between the two wars, including seven years of depression, it stayed practically the same.

But from 1939 to 1945, another war was fought and the debt increased again considerably; it increased sixfold, from $3,700 to $18,959 million in wartime. Out of this amount, several billions of dollars were given, not loaned, to England. I have often heard the hon. member for Villeneuve say that $7 billion were given to England during the war. And thus our debt went up from $3,710 to $18,959 million.

Since the war, there has been another period of peace, 20 or 22 years have gone by and this debt has remained practically stable, for it has increased from $18,959,000,000-as shown in the Statistical Yearbook for 1948-49-to $19,940,000,000, which is an increase of less than one billion in 22 years. The figure $19,940,000,000 is taken from the latest speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and may be found on page 195 of the official report for June 1, 1967.

Our debt, Mr. Speaker, was first made up of the debts of the other provinces which we assumed at the time of confederation in 1867, to which were simply added the expenses of the last four wars-the war waged by the British in South Africa, the 1914-18 war, the 1939-45 war, and the Korean war.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, our debt stands at $19,940 million and this year, we shall have to pay $1,274 million in interest only. The people of Quebec are paying 30 per cent of that amount. In 1942, at the time of the famous referendum on conscription, Quebec voted against it in a proportion of 90 per cent. And when Camilien Houde, then mayor of Montreal, objected, he was thrown in prison, without any trial or investigation. In the event of another war, the people of Quebec will have to accept it, whether they like it or not.
October 11, 1967
column2: COMMONS

column1: Even if the hon. member for Villeneuve is returned to the house and holds the balance of power with 50 members from Quebec, if we are led into the Viet Nam war, his power will be useless, since the 190 members from the other provinces will again side with England and the United States, which will add to our debt, even against the wishes and the aspirations of Quebec.

And if the member for Villeneuve raises strong protests, then he will have the same fate as Camilien Houde, he will be prosecuted and imprisoned. The balance of power will completely disappear before the majority of 190 members from the nine other provinces.

And on our present debt which we never wanted to incur, we are paying 30 per cent of the interests which amounted this year to $1,274 million, according to the figures quoted in the budget this year. A sum of $1,274 million and 30 per cent of that amount is paid each year by Quebeckers on a debt which they did not want to incur and which has never been of any use to them.

Now, what do the Quebeckers expect from the arms race or defence? We are a peace-loving people who would solve the world problems not with bombs and cannons but by feeding the hungry. That is the way we hope to co-operate in international operations.

But because we are a minority, every year the colossal national defence budget is imposed upon us and we have nothing to say about it: defence production, $38 million; national defence department, $1,688 million, a total of $1,726 million.
Just this year, we will be buying $26 million worth of bombs. What will Canada be doing with those bombs? On whose heads are those $26 million worth of bombs going to be thrown?

Yet, because we are a minority, because the taxes of the provinces are in the majority, we are forced to contribute through our taxes to such astronomical expenditures in the field of defence. If the two amounts for national defence and interest on the debt are added, we get the figure of three billion and some odd hundred thousand dollars a year. Therefore, our 30 per cent share, as we pay 30 per cent of the taxes levied by Ottawa, amounts to $900 million a year. That is what Quebec pays: $900 million a year. An independent Quebec would no longer have to face such extravagant expenditures, which we do not approve. We Quebeckers would then save a choice been made as to their destination? $900
DEBATES
The Budget-Mr. Gregoire million a year. Yes, mind you, $900 million a year.

Mr. Daniel Johnson, the premier of Quebec, tells us: Quebec has to borrow over $450 million each year. As the Quebec minister of industry says that investments in Quebec, in a given year, reach some $550 million, this means that Quebec gets 1 billion dollars, that is $450 million in foreign loans and $550 million in foreign investments.

If we could just save the fabulous sums of money being spent for defence and the interest on our debt, that would be equivalent, for Quebec only, to the share we are paying for that. Out of a total of $3 billion, our share amounts to $900 million. This would almost be sufficient, without changing anything else to enable us to become really independent from the economic point of view; that is if we, from Quebec, were politically independent and if we could decide once and for all, to stop giving away the money from our taxes to pay the astronomical amounts required by defence and by the interest on the national debt. Thus, there would be a saving of $900 million.

The other night, I heard the hon. member for Villeneuve say on TV: I am not independent if I am compelled to borrow money from the United States, I am dependent! That is a fact. We are compelled to borrow money from the United States, precisely because we have to pay the interest on the national debt, we have to buy bombs, submarines, munitions, we have to pay in connection with national defence the cost of armaments that will never be used. This is why we are economically dependent on a foreign power, and if we have an independent Quebec, we will put an end to such useless expenditures and, thus, win our economic independence.

No political independence without economic independence, that is true, but I also say: No economic independence without political independence. As long as Quebeckers are not free and are not able to decide on the purpose of their expenditures and their taxes, Ottawa will keep on spending as it does today, disregarding our views, and we shall remain economically dependent.

That is why I say that it is Ottawa's fault, as a result of its national budget, if today we are economically dependent, and if we get rid of that control by Ottawa, we shall become independent not only in the political sense but also economically.
October 11, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Coates

I admit that Quebeckers are not longing for constitutional changes, that they want to settle their economic problems; that is true. But we shall not be able to settle them as long as Ottawa controls the main decisions to be taken in the economic field and as long as it uses that control to impose upon us the kind of expenditures which we do not want.
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is why I say that the fault lies with Ottawa that we are at present in a constant state of dependence economically.

Confederation has been in existence for one hundred years. It is one hundred years since we are working, developing a little our natural resources, building industries, trying to train qualified people in Quebec; nevertheless, after one hundred years we are being told that Quebeckers need foreign investments since they have no savings, they have no means to develop their resources. The reason why we have nothing, why we have no savings is that they have been channelled to Ottawa and Ottawa has used them not to develop our own economy but for purposes such as I specifically mentioned a while ago and which are of no interest to us, are not at all in the interest of the population, and are even against its interests.

Coates (Cumberland):,,THE BUDGET,ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,Mr. Speaker, in entering this debate I feel certain there are many valid criticisms to be made about the economic policies of the present administration. However none is more devastating than the criticism of the lack of economic policy in so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned. By the time I have finished putting on the record some pertinent statistics relating to the economy of the Atlantic provinces there will be no member in this chamber who could disagree with me.

I also feel certain there are many hon. members who have come to the conclusion that members from the Atlantic provinces are almost chronic complainers; but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the statistics put out by the Atlantic provinces economic council-and I may mention that this is a non-partisan council which has no association with any political party-will verify beyond shadow of a doubt that the economy of the Atlantic provinces
has not received the kind of attention from this government that one would expect, if that region is to remain a strong and healthy part of this Canada of ours.

In this connection I refer to the July 1967 Atlantic report. Let me draw the attention of hon. members to some of the basic factors that one must consider when making a determination of the strength of the economy of a given area of this nation. First of all I should like to refer to personal incomes for the year 1966. In that year the people in the Atlantic provinces as a group had a personal income that was only 69.4 per cent of the national average-not a very flattering figure. What is even more alarming is that in 1961 the figure for the Atlantic provinces was 69 per cent of the national average; in other words, in five years personal incomes increased by only .4 per cent.

The picture is even worse, Mr. Speaker, when we look at the figures relating to Ontario, where we discover that the difference in per capita income between that province and the Atlantic provinces is 44.5 per cent. Surely it is next to impossible to expect the Atlantic provinces to survive as a basic part of this nation unless some sort of over-all policy is introduced to upgrade the income average of this particular area.

This is only one of many alarming statistics relating to the Atlantic provinces. For example, Mr. Speaker, may I point out at the same time that while the over-all per capita income of the people in the Atlantic provinces in 1966 was 69.4 per cent of the national average, in Newfoundland it was only 61.7 per cent and in Prince Edward Island it was only 64.8 per cent, which is below the average for the Atlantic provinces.

We are also facing a growing problem that should be of the utmost concern to this government but which seems to be of no concern to them, certainly if policy is any indication of concern. I refer to the exodus of people from our area. For many years we in the Atlantic provinces considered the present President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) the real bogeyman as far as the Liberal government was concerned. We called him oneway Gordon because he was the man to provide one-way tickets out of the region. He has been replaced by the whole Pearson administration and they are moving our people out as fast as they can, in the hope that they can eliminate our population. That is the policy of the present administration, and is the sole policy offered to cure our economic ills.
October 11, 1967

Let us look at statistics. The views I present are not my own but are those of the Atlantic provinces economic council. That body reports that between 1961 and 1966 more than 100,000 people, roughly 20,000 per year, migrated from the Atlantic provinces. This is the highest level of out migration that has ever been recorded for any five year period in the Atlantic provinces. Clearly, out migration from the region has reached alarming proportions. If that trend continues the Atlantic provinces will have lost 200,000 people by 1971, or 10 per cent of the 1961 population. Moreover, limited studies of this area show that the younger and more dynamic element, those who are best fitted to make a positive contribution to the region, are leaving in search of better opportunities elsewhere. I can think of nothing that ought to concern the government more than a statement to that effect by a non-political, nonpartisan economic body.

What is the result? Recently this government permitted the implementation of a new transport rate that is bound to cripple Atlantic provinces industries. This is the yardstick of the government's concern for our people. The people of the Atlantic provinces are concerned about a government that seems to go from crisis to crisis and seems to think that a crisis is commonplace. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) tells us that unless business and labour show restraint, the government's policy will be one of creating unemployment in Canada. His words, as reported on page 2809 of Hansard, are as follows:

I feel that we must-and we will-find some way to bring this inflationary movement under control even, if necessary, by letting the economy develop a little more slack for a year or two while price and cost increases taper off.

I ask the Minister of Finance, how much slack does he want in the Atlantic provinces? How hot is the economy of the Atlantic provinces, that it needs to be cooled off. The report of the Atlantic provinces economic council says this on the first page:

With the absence of any degree of growth in the total labour force the unemployment rate rose slightly from 9.3 per cent last year to 9.6 this year (double the national rates of 4.4 and 4.9 per cent respectively).
How much more unemployment must we take because of the fumbling and bumbling of this government? I am sure the people of the Atlantic provinces wish to know that.
The report shows that at 12 per cent Newfoundland's rate of unemployment was

The Budget-Mr. Coates the highest in the region. How much more slack do we need in Newfoundland? That province was followed by New Brunswick with 10.3 per cent, Prince Edward Island with 8.8 per cent and Nova Scotia with 7.8 per cent. Surely no government with any humanity would deliberately espouse policies that will create greater hardship for the Atlantic provinces than the figures I have quoted show must already exist. Nevertheless the Minister of Finance has said that his policy will be one of unemployment for the people of Canada, unless they show restraint. What example of that restraint did he show? In times of boom-and certainly the Atlantic provinces show no signs of boom-he says we are to have a deficit of $750 million.

2505982,ca.proc.d.1967-10-11.21.1.41,1967-10-11,f8c074be-3032-4ab6-af4f-11618169c92a,ca.m.8084,Mr. Coates:,,THE BUDGET,ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,The minister also talks about restraint. He came in the other day and told us a wonderful fairytale about the way in which he had slashed the estimates of the various departments. For this year?-not on your life. He had butchered the estimates for next year. Has anyone in this chamber seen those estimates? No, Mr. Speaker. This is just something he has done in his office, or in treasury board. I like Mr. John Meyer's account of the Minister of Finance slashing away at these estimates, as we read it in the October 6 edition of the Chronicle-Herald. Mr. Meyer says this:

The Treasury Board has trimmed $650 million from the requests for funds in the next fiscal year by departments and agencies. Mr. Sharp won't say where these reductions are being made. He does say there will be more of them.

It's encouraging to be told the government recognizes the need for restraint. Still, one is left with the same sense of unreality that must possess the husband whose wife tells him she has saved $100 by not buying a new dress-and asks for the money instead.

This is a good description of the way in which $650 million has disappeared from estimates we have never seen. The yardstick by which to gauge the degree of restraint exercised by this government should surely be a comparison between the spending this year and the next year's estimates. If the government intends to show restraint it ought to bring in estimates indicating a degree of selfdiscipline which has not been forthcoming any time from this administration so far, although hon. gentlemen opposite were well aware of the difficulties facing the country in a monetary sense.

I should like now to return to the subject of the Atlantic provinces. We were hopeful that a comprehensible policy would be forthcoming to give us grounds for optimism in the future. But there has been nothing to encourage such hopefulness. I should therefore like to make a suggestion to the government, one which, though containing some drawbacks from my own point of view, seems to represent the only kind of positive approach which can be expected at this time if we are to find lasting solutions which will be of over-all benefit to the region.

At one time I had hoped that the Atlantic Development Board would produce a comprehensive program for the Atlantic provinces, and that it would inject into the region the kind of capital needed to provide Canadians who live there with the same opportunities as are available to Canadians living in other

column1: parts of the country. However, this government relegated the Atlantic Development Board to the role of gap filler, and while the board has been effective within its limited scope it can no longer be regarded as a body capable of doing the job I had envisaged for it when it was established.

In these circumstances I should now like to see a special committee of the Senate set up to make a comprehensive study of the Atlantic region-a study similar to that carried out by the other house in connection with land use and aging. It is true that specific studies have been made in relation to coal and transportation, but I believe the time has come for an examination which would include all aspects of the economic life of the region. Coal and steel certainly form an integral part of the economic environment of the area, but these industries must be considered in conjunction, for example, with transportation, including port activities, vis-a-vis icebreaking on the St. Lawrence.

The agriculture industry in the Atlantic provinces is anything but prosperous. In the tourist industry, in fishing, in lumbering, the picture is the same. I believe the hon. Senators in the other place can carry out the kind of function I have suggested, and that a committee of the Senate would have an appreciation of the historical background of the Atlantic provinces as well as an understanding of what we should be trying to achieve. Such a committee would be much better than a royal commission. In my opinion we do not take sufficient advantage of what can be done by the other place. There are some tremendously capable and able men sitting in that chamber-men who have given us the basis for the kind of legislation which has been passed here in recent years in connection with land use and in connection with aging. I think they could do the job which is required of them. We should not waste even a day in having the committee set up, getting this work started and marshalling statistics such as those I have put on record in Hansard this afternoon.

I say this because no Canadian, no matter how prosperous he may be today, can feel happy or contented when he realizes the amount of hardship and suffering which exists in the Atlantic provinces. And no Canadian can feel that a government is fulfilling its obligations when it allows conditions such as these to persist. Let us start as quickly as we can and finish a job which has been with us for a hundred years.

Now, dealing with another subject, one which I have read about in the newspapers, I wish to say that as a Canadian nothing makes me angrier than to read of people who have stood in line for hours and hours, in the rain and cold, waiting admission to one of the Expo exhibits, only to have some V.I.P. force them to stay in line even longer. So far as I am concerned there is no justifiable reason for this. I do not think for one minute that this necessarily occurs at the request of a V.I.P. All too often it is due to some overzealous administrator.

Since the taxpayers of Canada have been responsible for achieving this wonderful thing called Expo, I believe that when they visit it they should not be held up by anybody. If administrators wish to cater to a V.I.P. then let them select an hour when the V.I.P.'s visit is not going to disturb people who have been standing in line for hours and hours. I do not like this, and I am sure most Canadians do not like it. I am sorry that during the last big week end of Expo administrators did not find another way of handling the problem.

I do not anticipate that there will be many more visits by V.I.P's to Expo, but that does not mean we should let the matter go and say nothing about it. I hope there will be no recurrence of this, and that when people go to Expo they will gain entry to the exhibits as quickly as possible, having waited in line to do so, without being upset by some V.I.P.
