2505983,ca.proc.d.1967-10-11.21.1.42,1967-10-11,6ab1d342-3030-459c-9751-639f09fada02,ca.m.6516,Mr. Max Saltsman (Waterloo South):,,THE BUDGET,ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,Mr. Speaker, I regret that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) is not in the chamber. I had hoped he would be present to listen to some of my remarks about this budget, but no doubt he will read in Hansard what I have to say.

I should like to start by paying the minister the compliment of at least being clear. His is not the kind of clarity that says anything, but it certainly is a clarity that demonstrates, perhaps inadvertently, the reason for the government's failure to solve the country's problems. Some people may still believe we have a government. They come into the House of Commons and see government benches occupied, and so are under the impression that the country is being governed. But when they read the statement on the budget made by the Minister of Finance their disillusionment should be complete. The government has abdicated its responsibilities, and throughout
October 11, 1967
The Budget-Mr. Saltsman the minister's speech defeatism rings out loudly and clearly.
I wish to refer back to some of the words used by the minister in his speech, as recorded in Hansard of October 2, at page 2730:
A country like Canada, with the most rapidly growing labour force in the world, is bound to have a housing problem.

I would suggest that a country like Canada, that wishes to manage its economy, is not bound to have a housing problem; is not bound to have anything it does not wish to have. If it has a government that is willing to take an interest, that is willing in a positive way to enter into the economic activity of the country, then it is not bound to have a housing problem. But as long as the government abdicates its responsibility the country will experience a continuing shortage of houses for people who require them.
In his speech the minister made another assumption when he said:

The first problem we have to deal with, if we are going to face up to the housing problem adequately and not in a partisan fashion, looking at the realities of the situation, is the shortage of capital or I might say, if you want to put it another way, the shortage of savings.

This is what the minister said, in spite of the fact that Canada has the highest rate of savings of any modern country, certainly of any country in the western world. The minister talked about a shortage of savings when he should have been talking about a misdirection, a misallocation of savings, and a wrong priority by the government as to how the savings of the Canadian people should be used. I think the minister will go down in history as the master of unfounded hypotheses, especially if his speeches as recorded in Hansard are examined.

When the minister stands up with that great assurance and aplomb that he commands in the house, he makes his words sound almost credible. But we have to read them in print, without his personality surrounding them, in order to get the complete and true significance of what he is saying. What emerges then is nonsense. What emerges is an indication of his refusal to use the instrument of government, as his government was elected to do on behalf of the people.

The minister has thrown up his hands in failure. He has been beaten by the marketplace. When the marketplace makes a decision the minister, with all the great resources at his command, finds he cannot go against the marketplace. If that is the case I do not

know why we need this government, at all. We might as well turn everything back to the marketplace, if that is going to be the attitude, and at least save ourselves some money. I assume the Canadian people elected a government to manage their affairs, but this does not seem to have met with the approval of the Minister of Finance.

Obviously there are things in the economy that we cannot always influence. I do not think we can blame the minister if the weather goes bad and we have a crop failure, or if international conditions beyond our control influence our economy. But having said that, let me emphasize that the vast majority of economic decisions that have to be made come under the influence of the Minister of Finance.

It is time that we in this country realized there is only one sovereignty, the sovereignty of the people as expressed through their parliament. It is not the market place that is sovereign, it is parliament acting on behalf of the people of Canada.

The question of sovereignty is of the greatest importance in this debate, because the minister apparently believes it is the market place that is sovereign and not the government of Canada. It is important in a number of ways, and although I am not prone to quote the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) on my behalf, I would like to quote one statement of his which has a great deal of merit and expresses fairly clearly the idea of sovereignty.
Dealing with the question of foreign ownership, in the Financial Post of July 15, 1967, the Minister of Trade and Commerce was reported as saying:
Whether or not it is used wisely in the economic program of the nation depends upon the extent to which the government defines the rules of the game.
In the final analysis it does not matter who owns the capital. It is the use to which it is put that counts, and this is a field in which the government can be the determining influence.

However, we have the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) who disagrees with the Minister of Trade and Commerce-and I think for very good reasons. While it is true that the economic sovereignty rests with the government, the President of the Privy Council knows that his party will not exercise that sovereignty and therefore seeks to change the direction of ownership in this country as an indirect way of attempting some control over our destiny. He hopes that Canadian owners will be more concerned
Oclober 11, 1967
column2: COMMONS

column1: about the future of the country than will foreign owners. I do not think there is any evidence to support him on that, but he at least must be given credit for attempting it. The misguidedness of his attempt stems from the lack of faith in his own party.

In this latter half of the twentieth century the fact of political sovereignty is becoming more and more apparent. There really is no more economic power. Now that we have a democratic system which has provided political parties through which the people can express their points of view, and which give them reasonable alternatives, it is quite possible for the government they elect to determine their economic destiny. Their destiny need not be left to the marketplace. There is no such thing as business, either domestic or foreign, saying to the Canadian government which represents the Canadian people that business will not act in the national interest. It is completely within the power of the government to ensure that it does.

I should like to make one thing clear. The marketplace and the free enterprise system can be very useful instruments for determining efficiency; they can be very helpful in respect of many of the every-day decisions which must be made. I do not look forward to such a massive intervention in our economy that we would find government in every phase of our activity. This is not necessary. What is necessary, however, is that in those areas where the free enterprise system does provide useful opportunities in this country there is a responsibility upon the government to see that it works properly. I would suggest to the government that, despite its so-called adherence to the free enterprise system, the market is not working to the benefit of the Canadian people. It could be working a great deal better.

There is one aspect of our lives which cannot be left to the marketplace, and that is the determination of values and priorities in our society. Whatever the value of the marketplace may be, it certainly cannot be the ultimate arbiter of what is important or valuable to our civilization. This must be the role of political sovereignty. I should like to quote another Liberal-and I am sorry the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) does not pay a little more attention to some of the more progressive elements in the Liberal party. I quote from the Montreal Star of June 10, 1967, where Mr. Kierans is reported as saying this:
Canada should assert the supremacy of politics over property as Aristotle defined the over-riding

The Budget-Mr. Saltsman
interest of the ""public"". For the past 200 years, Canada was ""traumatized"" by the outmoded thesis of Adam Smith and Karl Marx that property was supreme.

We had two choices, he said: First to estimate our productivity and then define our social aims; or second, to define our social aims, such as medicare, and ""then fight like hell to establish the productivity.""
I hope that this message will not be lost on the minister when the question of implementation of medicare arises. Mr. Kierans clearly indicates that he prefers the second method, and goes on to say:
Once we establish by public policy that the public interest is supreme money becomes something to control like anything else.

There is a real dilemma facing the minister. He says we have no money for housing and yet, as has been indicated by the Economic Council, we have the highest level of savings. I would suggest that it is not a matter of the lack of money or the absence of savings, but rather the absence of priorities in respect of how that money should be used. It is time that this government established some priority for the savings of Canadians. In Canada we have the highest capital investment per worker, and yet our productivity is 25 per cent to 30 per cent lower than that of other countries with less capital investment.

This is not a new problem although the Economic Council stressed it very strongly. It is one of the central points the council made. This has been said for years. We could go back to 1957 when this was stated by the Royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. It was stated that the problem of productivity in the Canadian economy was bad, and needed correction. It was also pointed out that we were suffering from badly organized and poorly specialized industries which could not compete in the way they should. In this ten year period nothing has been done to increase productivity.

I might qualify that. I see a few heads are raised, including that of the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury). One thing was done: We had the Canada-United States auto agreement. It was absolutely wrong to enter into this agreement. Again, it was an evasion of responsibility. It has worked in a fashion; I will not argue about this because the facts are available. What should not have been done in order to find a solution was to integrate our economy with that of the United States and reduce for all time the possibility of our taking independent action regarding one sector of our industry.
October 11, 1967

Perhaps the Minister of Industry had no alternative in respect of that particular industry, but I would deplore seeing many more of our industries integrated in that particular fashion. There are alternatives, but those alternatives require positive and strong action on the part of our government. We have inflation with unemployment. The Minister of Finance feels that he may have to increase unemployment in order to cure inflation. Surely he can come up with a better answer than that. Surely this is not the only way to take care of the problem of inflation.

2505990,ca.proc.d.1967-10-11.21.1.49,1967-10-11,6ab1d342-3030-459c-9751-639f09fada02,ca.m.6516,Mr. Saltsman:,,THE BUDGET,ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,We have in this country, as everyone agrees, the highest growth potential of any country in the world. We have raw materials beyond anyone's expectation; we have wealth beyond calculation. There is no country in the world which has the wealth in agriculture, minerals and human resources that we have in this country. There is no other country in the world that is as self-reliant as Canada could be, or as independent of the whims and changes in the international markets. If we are dependent to some extent today, it is because this government has burdened us with this dependency. There is some conventional wisdom which must be examined. It is the assumption that we must export, export, and then export again.
[Mr. Saltsman.!

Let me suggest to the minister and the Minister of Industry-and I am glad to see him in the house today-that the effect of exporting raw materials from this country has resulted in a lack of secondary manufacturing industries we might have developed ourselves. This has turned us into a nation of exporters of raw materials at relatively low profit rather than a great nation of secondary manufacturers. This error on the part of the government has done a disservice to Canadians. This is the kind of conventional wisdom that should be examined.

Many of our exports consist of raw materials, and in many cases tremendous advantage is gained through exportation. The exportation of wheat has been a great boon to this country, as has the export of lumber. These are renewable resources. However, when we export resources such as nickel, only to find that the costs of exploration are increasing, this is not in the best interest of the country. Canada is known throughout the world for its production of nickel, yet Canadian manufacturers cannot get enough nickel to fulfil their own requirements. Let me read from an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail on March 3, 1967.
Because of government encouragement to seek export orders, Zenith has spent considerable money developing new products for U.S. sales.
This was a quotation from Mr. Laws, president of Zenith. The article then continues the quotation as follows:
Mr. Laws said he is faced with a shortage of nickel. ""I don't think we should be on a quota at all.""
Mr. Laws said the national economy would be better served by the export of finished products, rather than shipping out large quantities of raw nickel.

I believe he is right. Certainly there is no excuse for not satisfying the domestic market before exporting raw materials. This is not the first time this has occurred. It has occurred on other occasions which resulted in the shortage of copper and other minerals. We have been terribly concerned about satisfying export markets and not concerned enough with building up secondary industry.
It was interesting to read the minister's remarks of October 4 as recorded at page 2808 of Hansard, when he said:
We have never encountered anything like this before, nor has any other country. We are moving out now on to unexplored territory.
I am surprised the minister has such a short memory. It is my understanding that he

2505992,ca.proc.d.1967-10-11.21.1.51,1967-10-11,6ab1d342-3030-459c-9751-639f09fada02,ca.m.6516,Mr. Saltsman:,,THE BUDGET,ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE,,We are at war, and you should real se that fact. We have a war that must be fought against poverty. Many people need houses. Many young couples are being thrown out of apartment buildings because they have two or more children and landlords do not like to have children around. This may not appear to be a war to the minister, but it certainly is a war so far as those people who are struggling to maintain some sort of decent standard of living are concerned. I suggest that the minister take a very serious look at their plight instead of just saying that this is not a time of war. If we can muster our intelligence, resources and courage in order to devastate things, surely we can find some ingenuity to fight these problems of poverty.

The minister has said that solutions to our problems would not be easy to find. We must move away from reliance on past economic policies. We cannot continue to believe that if we wait things will adjust themselves. We have passed that point. Once we have committed ourselves to a full employment policy-and I do not see how any government could fail to follow such a policy-we must then go on further. We cannot turn the clock back to times of unemployment. We must talk about how to maintain prosperity and how to prevent inflation with full employment. In order to do this the government must bring in some measure of control over the economy.

There is no invisible hand to guide the destiny of the people. There are hands but they are not invisible-they are the hands of everyone looking toward his own interests. This may not be in the best interests of the people of this country, but it is the situation. There is no longer a question as to whether we are going to plan or not plan. The question now is, who is going to do the planning for us, the large corporations or the government. Are these large corporations to determine our economic future? I do not ask that question with any malevolence, but I feel that our economic future should be determined by the sovereign government elected by the people of this country. Does this government intend to sit here and suggest that it cannot interfere in these delicate matters, and
DEBATES
The Budget-Mr. F. E. Leblanc that the invisible hands will straighten things out?

In closing let me suggest that we cannot continue in the manner we have followed up to this time. We cannot rely on automatic forces to take care of things. The government is going to have to offer some direction and plan in order to maintain full employment in this country and the standard of living that is necessary. I suggest that we will need a prices review board, selected price controls, restructuring of our industry and a changing emphasis from primary to secondary manufacturing. The government must maintain more control on our economy and import replacement. There must be a lessening of our dependence on United States markets in order that we may determine our own values with less inhibition. In this way the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) will not have to say we can do nothing about foreign policy because 60 per cent of our exports go to the United States. That is not the way to determine foreign policy, and certainly not the right way to run a country.

We must implement the Carter Commission recommendations as soon as possible in order to have a better allocation of resources, instead of backtracking at the first sign of pressure. We must make available to all our manufacturers those raw materials which are indigenous to this country. Their needs must be satisfied first. Above all, we need an investment policy because the market can no longer determine the allocation of investment. It is this government, or any other government that wishes to accept responsibility, which must determine the social priorities and investment priorities of this nation. Above all, there must be a clear expression on the part of this government, elected by the people, that it will use the authority of government on behalf of those who sent them here and entrusted them with the direction of this country's future.

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the request of the Minister of Finance, intermediate bodies have started to submit their views on the report of the Carter royal commission.

The Carter royal commission is probably the most important commission called upon to report since confederation, that is, in a hundred years, in order to determine the existing or desirable standard of living in Canada. I have the greatest respect and admiration for the competence and the merits of its members.
Even though the commission did a good job, a tremendous job, the government must consider carefully all its recommendations before accepting or rejecting them.

However, I regret that the commission submitted its report in such a dictatorial way, warning that it must be accepted in toto or rejected in toto. That report has been and will again be very controversial throughout Canada, and I do not think it is democratic to force the parties concerned to accept or reject in bulk without further ado.

Economists, accountants, lawyers and all the others concerned with this problem do not seem to agree on the doctrinal and very theorical arguments set forth in the report, which advocates extreme changes, a complete fiscal revolution and an entirely new philosophy.

The assessment of the proposals about the national economy is so speculative and so unreliable that it seems improper and unthinkable that the government should accept that report in toto. According to that report, our present fiscal system as a whole is basically unsound judging from the sweeping structural changes it recommends.
Its criticism is very harsh, but I am not fully convinced that our present system is absolutely and entirely bad and that it must be scrapped.
[Mr. Leblanc (Laurier).J

Mr. Carter and his colleagues attempted to reject the past, that is to say all that is found now in the taxation field. They studied the problem as if it were necessary to start from scratch and, in my opinion, that underlines both the wisdom and the weakness of some recommendations.

Of course, our system is not perfect. It has often been patched up rather than revised according to an over-all plan. Needless to say, I am in favour, as all the members are, of lower taxes for the small wage-earner so that he might meet his basic requirements.
At the present time, those who earn less than $5,000 pay too much tax, compared to the other taxpayers, and the Minister of Finance should make the required adjustment.

Still, the whole burden should not be placed on the shoulders of those citizens who earn from $5,000 to $10,000, thereby creating another injustice while wanting to remedy the first error. In this regard, I have no concrete solution to offer, because the members unfortunately do not have at their disposal a staff of experts and researchers.

However, I am pleased to propose that the small wage-earner should have some relief and I urge the Minister of Finance to study the possibility of spreading out his taxes amongst other taxpayers whose income might justify higher taxes.

Mr. Speaker, I must speak up against one of the recommendations of the Carter commission. I have already done so in the house, on April 21, 1966, at which time I spoke on the same recommendation as made by the Belanger commission on the fiscal system in Quebec that the government should tax capital gains.

At the present time, in Canada and in Quebec, the citizen who has invested his savings in personal property or real estate the value of which increases over a certain period of time, pays no tax on this capital gain when he sells them.

If the recommendation of the commission were accepted by the government, that tax would be imposed on this appraisal of capital. Under the present system, a gain realized on assets which are considered as an investment is regarded as capital and is therefore not taxable. But if a gain realized on assets comes from some business activity, it is regarded as income and is therefore taxable.
One of the disastrous effects of taxation on capital gain would occur at the time of death when the increase in value of the assets of the deceased, compared with its original cost,

would be subject to an additional estates tax. That is, in my opinion, a sure way, sooner or later, to liquidate our family businesses, thereby promoting the control of foreign capital over the business of our country.

It seems inconsistent to suggest such a tax, since Canada is not ready to pass that kind of legislation. It would be contrary to common sense to tax directly the people who are prepared to risk some capital in Canadian business while our country is still in the first stages of its economic development. I fail to see how we can attract capital by imposing a tax on capital gain.

I do not agree with the commission, which believes this tax to be equitable and necessary. In a democracy, all citizens are equal in the eyes of the law, and all have an equal chance to develop their talents. This does not mean that all are equally gifted, that knowledge and experience are not worth more than ignorance and lack of experience, nor that the judgement of any one person is better than that of the rest, or that all opinions are equally good. The possession of material wealth is like the possession of talent. It varies from one individual to the next, and in my opinion it would be unfair to penalize the richer man. Instead, we should try to redistribute wealth in the best interests of the whole population.

An almost wild territory could not ensure the development of its natural resources without large investments involving of course great risks. In this connection, I refer the house to the statistics which show that there are more business failures per capita in Canada than elsewhere.

It should not be overlooked that Canada must gather investment capital, especially in this century, and that such legislation could scare away the capital needed to develop our resources. It is beyond understanding that a country as greatly and urgently in need of capital as ours would accept a capital gains tax.
If we wish to stop the influx of Canadian or foreign capital, and to discontinue and suspend the fantastic development of our economy, we have only to levy a capital gains tax.

Canada is not ready yet to assume such a tax burden, as it still needs the massive influx of foreign capital to insure its development and to create new employment opportunities, of which Canadians are in urgent need.

There is no doubt that the effect of a capital gains tax would be to restrict the free flow of capital and, especially, to reduce the amounts available to initiate or expand high risk developments. It would also discourage sound savings, keep away investments of capital so important for our development and prompt our own investors to transfer their assets to more friendly lands especially at a time where we are unfortunately experiencing a serious brain drain for the benefit of more attractive economic climates.

In other countries where the economy is sufficiently mature and productive to support that burden, such tax is in force and can be levied. The principles brought forward by the Carter commission might apply later on when the country has an adequate population and has reached adulthood with a parallel economic development.

It is true that the United States and Great Britain levy such a tax. In this connection, however, I should like to quote Mr. Henry C. Wallick, professor of economics at Yale University and former assistant to the American secretary to the treasury, who speaks about the harmful eflect of that tax as follows:

A capital gains tax affects the supply of saving much more severely than would a true income tax of identical yield...A capital gains tax not being a tax upon what can properly be considered income, is paid very largely out of savings, or out of capital which amounts to the same thing... the principal adverse effect... is that on saving. The tax absorbs a not insignificant part of the annual supply of saving. For an economy trying to maximize its rate of growth, almost any other method of raising revenue would have less counterproductive effects-

Do not forget that if we tax capital gains, capital losses will obviously have to be allowed as a deduction. What would be the net revenue from this tax, and is it really worthwhile? If the results of inflation are taken into account when assessing capital gains, I doubt that the actual capital gains would be as high as the Carter commission hopes. And how can we justly impose a tax on inflated values?
Let us not forget that the possibility of deducting a capital loss from other revenues is not as strong an incentive as the possibility of retaining an increase which all Canadians seek.
